item.content:encoded:
This week open models closed in and agents learned to ask first. Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro comes within a point of Claude Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, with weights promised by 4 November, and Recursive released a 40B open coding model that runs on a laptop. Anthropic previewed Claude Duet, an always-on agent that waits for approval before it sends, pays or signs, while FrontierCS 2 found that the best coding agent beats a research paper's own code in 58% of runs. On the systems side, llm-d reached 1.0 for cache-aware serving on Kubernetes, Meta sized a 30B agent model for one 32 GB GPU, and encoders as small as 17M parameters chose tools on a CPU in 13.5 ms.

Read the full interactive issue on yathishreddy.github.io →
Each pick below links to its card with the key figure, results table and technical deep dive.

LLMs & language models

The week's largest release came from Moonshot: Kimi K3.1 Pro comes within a point of Claude Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 37% of its cost per task in tbench.ai data, and its weights are due by 4 November. Recursive released Flint, an Apache-licensed 40B expert model for local coding that it says its own research system largely built. On the research side, Lafa shows that continuous flow models adapted from existing chat models can draft and self-verify text 2.5 times faster than standard decoding.

Kimi K3.1 Pro: a 3T-class model that matches Opus 5.5 on terminal coding, with weights promised

Moonshot AI · 23 Oct · model · API · weights soon

TL;DR: Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro is a heavily post-trained Kimi K3 with a 1M-token context. It nearly matches Claude Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and weights are due by 4 November.

65.7% Terminal-Bench 4.0 (Moonshot-reported), against 66.4% for Claude Opus 5.5 and 58.2% for GPT-6 Astra

Why it matters: If the weights arrive as promised, the strongest openly downloadable model will sit within a point of Claude Opus 5.5 on terminal coding, and Artificial Analysis already ranks it 55, behind only Opus 5.5 at 58.

Read with care: Most scores are Moonshot's own and use its choice of harnesses, several key comparisons rely on internal benchmarks, and the weights and licence were not yet public at launch.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Lafa: a flow language model that drafts blocks of text and checks them itself, 2.5 times faster

UC Berkeley · Amazon · KAIST · Carnegie Mellon University · 20 Oct · paper · code · models

TL;DR: Lafa turns a pretrained 7–8B chat model into a flow model that generates token blocks in parallel and verifies them with its own next-token predictions, using under 30B training tokens.

2.54× throughput of the matched 7B autoregressive model on one H100 at comparable accuracy (authors' measurement)

Why it matters: It shows that continuous flow models, so far limited to small experiments, can be built cheaply from existing chat models and beat multi-token prediction and discrete diffusion on the speed–quality trade-off.

Read with care: Speed was measured only at batch size one on short benchmarks (generation capped at 1,024 tokens), and one- or two-step flow-map decoding without verification still loses accuracy against multi-step flow.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Flint: a 40B open coding model that Recursive says was largely built by its own research system

Recursive · 21 Oct · model · weights

TL;DR: Recursive's first model, Flint, is a 39.8B mixture-of-experts coder with about 2.5B active parameters per token, released under Apache 2.0 and sized for a single GPU or a laptop.

89.7% SWE-bench Pro v2 (Recursive-reported), with about 2.5B of 39.8B parameters active per token

Why it matters: It is a fully open, Apache-licensed coding model small enough to run on a laptop, and an early public test of a lab claiming that AI systems did much of the model-building work.

Read with care: All scores are Recursive's own with no independent evaluation yet, and neither the model card nor coverage explains what the Eureka Machine actually did or how much of the work it automated.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Vision models

This week's vision papers share one idea: give generative models explicit structure rather than hoping it emerges from pixels. VPM shows that forecasting 3D point trajectories improves multi-view video and robot control, Matrix-Game 4.0 hands game state to an engine so a distilled video model only has to paint, and RoAR-VAE makes latents easier for diffusion models to learn by keeping meaning and detail recoverable under noise.

Video-Point Model: a world model that forecasts where every point will move

KAIST · ETH Zürich · New York University and partners · 20 Oct · paper · benchmark

TL;DR: VPM forecasts multi-view future video together with 3D trajectories of scene points. Point supervision improves video quality, 3D consistency and real-robot success over a video-only version.

79.2% real-robot banana pick-and-place success with point supervision, against 58.3% without it (24 trials each)

Why it matters: It gives evidence that asking a video world model to predict explicit 3D motion makes its pictures more consistent across cameras and its robot policies more reliable, at almost no extra inference cost.

Read with care: Training trajectories come from simulation, the real-robot tests cover only three pick-and-place tasks with 24 trials each, and all comparisons are the authors' own.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Matrix-Game 4.0: a game engine keeps the rules while a video model paints the frames

SkyworkAI · CUHK · UC San Diego and partners · 20 Oct · paper · code · weights

TL;DR: Matrix-Game 4.0 lets a light game engine hold world state and rules, and a distilled video model repaint its low-poly frames at 480p, 60 FPS on one RTX 5090.

112 ms key-press-to-display latency on one RTX 5090 at 480p, against about 517 ms for the next-fastest system compared

Why it matters: Moving rules and memory out of the video model and into code addresses the drift and forgetting of pure video world models, and the speed work shows such neural rendering can run on one consumer GPU.

Read with care: One renderer is trained per game on purpose-made Unreal Engine data, there are no quantitative image-quality metrics against other systems, and the latency comparison mixes resolutions and hardware.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

RoAR-VAE: an image tokeniser that matches FLUX.2's VAE using only ImageNet

Tsinghua University · Microsoft Research · 19 Oct · paper · code

TL;DR: RoAR-VAE trains an image autoencoder so that semantics and pixels stay recoverable from noise-corrupted latents. Diffusion models learn faster on it, and small text survives reconstruction better.

63.86 average of GenEval, GenEval2 and DPG-Bench after 32k training steps, 2.19 above the best baseline tokeniser

Why it matters: The tokeniser sets the ceiling for every latent image and video model, and this gives an open, simple recipe for one that is both easy to learn on and good at preserving text and faces.

Read with care: All tests are at 256×256 with a 0.8B diffusion model trained for 32k steps, so behaviour at the resolutions and scales of production systems is untested.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Agentic AI

The agent story this week runs from product to measurement to training. Anthropic joined Meta and OpenAI with an always-on personal agent that must ask before it sends, pays, signs or deletes, while a Berkeley-led benchmark found that the best coding agent beats published research code in 58% of runs. On the training side, Microsoft Research and partners showed that open models alone can build the simulated computers and verified tasks needed to improve computer-use agents with RL.

FrontierCS 2: can coding agents beat the code that came with a research paper?

UC Berkeley · Princeton University · Scale AI and partners · 21 Oct · benchmark · code

TL;DR: FrontierCS 2 deletes a paper's contribution from its own repository and asks agents to rebuild it better. Across 48 tasks in 13 domains, the best agent passes 58% of runs.

58% pass rate for Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, the best of 12 agents; no agent passes 16 of the 48 tasks

Why it matters: It tests the step from fixing issues to improving research systems, across databases, security, networking, HPC and robotics as well as machine learning, against real published code rather than a rubric.

Read with care: Each agent ran each task only once, every model is tied to one harness, and the authors' own case studies show that pass and score can miss what matters, such as circuit size or how many bytes a run saved.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Claude Duet: Anthropic's always-on agent that asks before it acts

Anthropic · 21 Oct · product · research preview

TL;DR: Anthropic opened a research preview of Claude Duet, an Opus 5.5 app that watches connected accounts, works in its own cloud browser and asks before consequential actions.

6,000+ connectors and plugins Duet can use, carried over from the user's Claude account (reported by Anthropic)

Why it matters: It is Anthropic's entry into proactive personal agents, after Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots, and makes approval gates and credential isolation part of the product rather than an afterthought.

Read with care: It is an early preview with no published error rates, Anthropic acknowledges it can misjudge what is urgent, and the claude.com announcement could not be read in this run, so details come from press coverage.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

WildAWM: training computer-use agents in synthetic worlds built only by open models

UNC Chapel Hill · Microsoft Research · Georgia Tech · Northeastern University · 19 Oct · paper · code · data

TL;DR: WildAWM uses open models to build simulated personal computers with websites, MCP services and files, plus verified tasks. RL there lifts Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 10.6 points on eight unseen benchmarks.

+10.58 average points gained by Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on eight out-of-distribution agent benchmarks (reported by the authors)

Why it matters: Environment supply is now a bottleneck for agent RL, and this shows that open models alone can produce long, verifiable, cross-interface tasks that still challenge frontier models (GPT-6-Astra passes about 60%).

Read with care: Gains concentrate where the GLM-5.2 teacher can already succeed, the trained 35B model remains about 20 points behind frontier models, and some benchmarks use subsets (99 of 330 OSWorld tasks).

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

On-device inference

This week's on-device work is about fitting agents into consumer memory and power budgets. Meta's Muse Glimmer publishes its own 4-bit recipes and drafter, Tandem shows that checkpoint placement and NPU power states decide phone-agent latency and battery, and a MacPaw study warns that server-GPU speedups, especially speculative decoding, often do not carry over to Apple Silicon.

Muse Glimmer 30B: Meta's open agent model sized for one 32 GB consumer GPU

Meta Superintelligence Labs · 17 Oct · catch-up · model · weights · report

TL;DR: Meta released Muse Glimmer, a dense 30B text-and-image model distilled from Muse Spark under Apache 2.0, with 4-bit weights under 20 GB and a DFlash speculative-decoding drafter.

75.6% 15-task average for the EvoPress 4-bit build, against 75.7% for BF16 (Meta-reported)

Why it matters: It is a frontier-lab model built from the start for local agents, with the quantisation choices and drafter published rather than left to the community.

Read with care: The report states that the model runs at practical speeds on a single RTX 5090 but gives no measured tokens per second or drafter acceptance rates, and all benchmark scores are Meta's own.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Tandem: a phone GUI agent on the Snapdragon NPU, 28% faster and a third less energy per step

Florida International University · University of Houston · NEC Labs America · Singapore Management University · 19 Oct · paper · code

TL;DR: Tandem adapts llama.cpp's Hexagon NPU backend to hybrid linear-attention agents such as Qwen3.5-4B, cutting step latency by 28%, energy by 33% and loaded standby power from 0.76 to 0.22 W.

10.1 J energy above idle per text step on a Snapdragon 8 Elite, against 15.1 J for llama.cpp's fastest NPU setup

Why it matters: On-device agents run many short steps with idle gaps, and this shows that checkpoint placement, rollback cost and NPU power state, not raw decode speed, decide latency and battery life.

Read with care: Results are for one fine-tuned 4B policy, Chinese apps and two Snapdragon phones; Mamba2 layers still fall back to the CPU, and screenshot steps gain only 13–17% because the vision encoder dominates.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Which GPU tricks survive on a Mac: KV pruning helps, speculative decoding mostly does not

MacPaw AI&Research · Lviv Polytechnic National University · 22 Oct · paper

TL;DR: A study on four Apple Silicon Macs finds KV-cache pruning speeds local inference by up to 1.75×, while six speculative decoding methods all lost throughput on the main chat benchmark.

0.38× DFlash decode throughput on an M3 Ultra (156.7 to 60.0 tok/s), despite 3.57 tokens per round

Why it matters: It gives Mac users and runtime developers measured evidence on which published speedups to expect locally, rather than assuming server-GPU results carry over.

Read with care: KV pruning was measured for speed only, not output quality, and different runtimes per method mean the speculative-decoding losses cannot be attributed to the hardware alone.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

SLMs under 1B parameters

No major lab released a sub-1B model this week, so the column follows three ways small models are being put to work. Encoders from 17M to 400M parameters make closed-set routing and tool choices without an LLM call, a Qwen3-0.6B learns to screen phone calls from synthetic data, and a 135M language model becomes a speech recogniser that invents far fewer words.

Crivo: 17M to 400M encoders that pick tools and route requests on a CPU

Federal Institute of São Paulo (IFSP) · 22 Oct · paper · weights · code

TL;DR: Crivo encoders score every option in one pass. The 68M and 150M models beat a 435M DeBERTa zero-shot classifier on 209 tasks; the 17M answers in 13.5 ms on CPU.

13.5 ms median CPU latency of the 16.9M Crivo-17M per request (16 threads), against 728 ms for DeBERTa-v3-large (authors' figures)

Why it matters: An encoder of 17M to 150M parameters that routes requests or picks tools in tens of milliseconds on an ordinary CPU removes an LLM call from many agent loops.

Read with care: Reordering the options changes 12–23% of answers, the models are over-confident on unseen tasks and near the floor on the leaderboard's new-domain tests, and the weights are CC BY-NC 4.0.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Teaching a Qwen3-0.6B call-screening agent to reply safely and summarise calls

Scam.ai · 18 Oct · paper

TL;DR: A LoRA adapter trained on 3,395 synthetic calls lifts Qwen3-0.6B from 20.8% to 94.8% qualified replies and from 2.1% to 51.6% qualified owner summaries, as judged by an LLM evaluator.

94.8% qualified in-call replies from Qwen3-0.6B after adaptation, up from 20.8% (192 held-out calls, authors' evaluator)

Why it matters: It shows that most of the gap between a sub-1B model and a usable on-device phone agent is training data, not size: the 0.6B model's reply rate ends within 2 points of the 4B model's.

Read with care: The same GPT-6 Astra model screened the training data and scored the outputs, so the rates measure agreement with that evaluator, not human acceptance; no data or weight release is stated.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

AudioSLM: a SmolLM2-135M speech recogniser that invents far fewer words

National Taiwan Normal University · 18 Oct · paper · code

TL;DR: Speech models built on language models insert words nobody said. AudioSLM adds CTC alignment cues and cross-attention to a SmolLM2-135M backbone, cutting the hallucinated-word rate from 52.01% to 8.69%.

8.69% hallucination error rate on LibriSpeech dev-clean with SmolLM2-135M, down from 52.01% for the plain design (authors' figures)

Why it matters: It gives a sub-200M language-model back-end for on-device transcription that beats a 7B-guided decoder on noisy speech and shows that smaller backbones hallucinate less.

Read with care: It is tested only on read English LibriSpeech with 100 hours of training, the slightly lower correct-word rate is a trade-off, and the paper does not state the full system's parameter count or run it on a device.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

AI infrastructure

The week's infrastructure news was about the KV cache as the unit of cost. llm-d reached 1.0 as a shared layer that routes by cached prefix and tiers the cache to SSD, a Tsinghua paper let agents prune their own cache without recomputation, and Snowflake showed what it takes to fit long-horizon RL for a new hybrid model on one training node.

llm-d 1.0: an open Kubernetes stack for cache-aware, disaggregated LLM serving

CNCF llm-d project (Google Cloud · Red Hat · IBM · CoreWeave · NVIDIA and partners) · 20 Oct · release · open source

TL;DR: llm-d reached 1.0 under the CNCF, routing requests to replicas that already hold their KV cache and splitting prefill, decode and encode into separate pools on GPUs and TPUs.

2.4× total throughput over a plain Kubernetes Service on an agentic coding workload on Ironwood TPUs, reported by Google

Why it matters: It turns the serving techniques that recent issues covered one engine at a time (prefix caching, disaggregation, KV offload) into a shared, vendor-neutral control layer that Google, CoreWeave, DigitalOcean and JetBrains already run in production.

Read with care: Every number comes from launch posts by the project's own backers, each against a different baseline, and the largest cost claims (5–10× cheaper than commercial APIs) rest on stated rental-price assumptions.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Cache engineering: agents that drop parts of their own KV cache instead of summarising

Tsinghua University · The Chinese University of Hong Kong · 20 Oct · paper · code

TL;DR: Agents drop old tool outputs from the KV cache rather than rewriting the conversation, so nothing is recomputed. The AKV server on SGLang cuts average cost by 27.7%.

−27.7% average cost against threshold summarisation, with average scores 1.7 points higher (three models, four benchmarks)

Why it matters: KV-cache reads make up 82.4% of API cost in the authors' agent traces, and this moves cache management from the server's hidden heuristics into something the agent can control and the server can still reuse correctly.

Read with care: Experiments use older A800 GPUs at BF16 with API-price cost estimates, gains are uneven (GPT-OSS-120B scores one point lower on xbench-DeepSearch), and linear-attention models are not yet supported.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

FlashNext-RL: agentic RL on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with one training node

Snowflake AI Research · 20 Oct · paper

TL;DR: Snowflake trains the 125B Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with RL on one 8×B200 node at 131K-token context, raising trainer throughput from about 395 to 4,438 tokens/s per GPU.

22.4 min per RL step of 1,024 trainable software-engineering rollouts, on one training and three inference nodes

Why it matters: It is a rare, fully itemised account of what it takes to run long-horizon agent RL on a new open hybrid model, showing that architecture-specific kernels and memory planning, not the RL algorithm, decide whether it fits on available hardware.

Read with care: The study covers one model on one node type, the live run lasted only 15 steps with no reported accuracy gain, and several components (first two layers, n-gram table, indexer, MTP head) were frozen.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

item.title: Issue 04: Big models come closer to the desk
item.dc:creator: Yathish Reddy
item.description:
This week's theme is where models run. Meta released an 816B open-weight model that fits on two Mac Studios, Liquid AI's 24B expert model decodes at 184 tokens a second on a laptop, and a 1.2B call assistant runs on phone chips for millions of users. Two infrastructure reports put AMD GPUs level with NVIDIA's for serving and training, and agent research turned to scale and trust: 30,000 agent merges a day, and verifiers hardened against cheating agents.

item.content:encoded:
This week's theme is where models run. Meta released an 816B open-weight model that fits on two Mac Studios, Liquid AI's 24B expert model decodes at 184 tokens a second on a laptop, and a 1.2B call assistant runs on phone chips for millions of users. Two infrastructure reports put AMD GPUs level with NVIDIA's for serving and training, and agent research turned to scale and trust: 30,000 agent merges a day, and verifiers hardened against cheating agents.

Read the full interactive issue on yathishreddy.github.io →
Each pick below links to its card with the key figure, results table and technical deep dive.

LLMs & language models

Meta returned to the frontier with Muse Wonder, a closed model for long-running agents, and released the weights of Muse Spark Open, an 816B expert model that runs on two Mac Studios. NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is less strong on benchmarks but ships with its training data and recipes.

Muse Wonder: Meta's first frontier-class models, built for long-running agents

Meta Superintelligence Labs · 12 Oct · model · API

TL;DR: Meta released Muse Wonder and Wonder Full, closed models with a 1M-token context. In Meta's own table, Wonder Full leads long-horizon coding but trails Claude Opus 5.5 elsewhere.

57.5% SWE-Marathon, Muse Wonder Full (Meta-reported), against 46.3% for Claude Opus 5.5

Why it matters: It puts Meta back among the frontier labs on agent and coding benchmarks, with independent measurements from Artificial Analysis placing Wonder Full at 56 on its index, behind Opus 5.5 at 58.

Read with care: Meta discloses no parameter count or architecture, most scores are Meta's own, and the strongest model, Wonder Full, cannot be called through the API at all.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Muse Spark Open: an 816B open-weight model that fits on two Mac Studios

Meta Superintelligence Labs · 15 Oct · model · weights

TL;DR: Meta published the weights of Muse Spark Open, an 816B mixture-of-experts model with 42B active parameters and a 1M-token context. Its quantised form runs on two 512 GB Mac Studios.

89.2 MCP-Atlas, the top score among the eight open-weight models in Meta's table

Why it matters: It is the strongest US open-weight model in Meta's comparison and the first frontier-scale Meta weights since the Llama line, available from day one on seven clouds and six inference engines.

Read with care: The licence is not open source in the OSI sense, the full evaluation report was still "available soon", and Chinese open models remain ahead on the overall index and on coding.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL: a 120B open hybrid model released with its data and recipes

NVIDIA · 14 Oct · model · weights · data

TL;DR: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B Mamba-transformer expert model with 12B active and image and video input. Weights, training data and recipes are public.

2.43× NVFP4 throughput over BF16, keeping 99.62% median accuracy across 36 benchmarks

Why it matters: It is one of the few large models released with pretraining and post-training data and full recipes, so others can study or reproduce how a competitive agentic model is built.

Read with care: All numbers are NVIDIA's own, and on most coding and agent benchmarks in its own table the model trails Qwen, GLM and DeepSeek models of similar size.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Vision models

Two vision papers remove work that models were doing by habit: writing out answers a video model could score directly, and running a slow teacher to get a one-step image generator. Datalab's Indra OCR shows how far document reading can shrink, to a recogniser of about 1M parameters that needs no GPU.

VideoJev: video models that score answers instead of writing them

Nanjing University · JD.com · Tsinghua University and partners · 13 Oct · paper · code · models

TL;DR: VideoJev replaces a video model's text output with a head that scores candidate time spans and answer options, reusing one video encoding. It answers over 100× faster than reasoning baselines.

129× faster per question than Qwen3.5-4B Thinking on LVBench, at a 0.6-point lower four-benchmark mean

Why it matters: Video agents mostly need quick, structured judgements about the same footage (when did this happen, which option is true), and this shows those can be made in one pass without generating text.

Read with care: It only answers questions with a fixed set of candidates, not open-ended ones, and the question-answering data is an internal corpus of about 240K questions that is not described as released.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Priming Models: one-step image generators trained with a tenth of the compute

Seoul National University · Harvard University · 14 Oct · paper · code

TL;DR: Pretraining a generator simply to denoise images at one fixed noise level, then matching feature distributions, gives a one-step ImageNet FID of 1.19 using 238.95 EFLOPs of training compute.

FID 1.19 ImageNet 256×256 in one network pass (authors' evaluation), 238.95 EFLOPs of training

Why it matters: One-step generators are much cheaper to run than diffusion models, and this recipe removes most of the training tricks and teacher models they have needed.

Read with care: Results are mostly at research scale (a 258M-parameter text-to-image model at 512×512), and the one-step text-to-image model still trails a 100-step flow-matching baseline (GenEval 0.818 against 0.873).

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Indra OCR: a 1M-parameter text recogniser that reads 49 pages a second on CPU

Datalab · 13 Oct · code · weights

TL;DR: Indra OCR pairs a recogniser of about 1M parameters with layout detection. Datalab reports 49.4 pages a second on 32 CPU cores, beating PaddleOCR text models and Tesseract.

49.4 pages/s on 32 AMD EPYC cores with no GPU, reported by Datalab

Why it matters: Fast CPU-only OCR is the first step of many document and retrieval pipelines, and a model this small removes the need for a GPU at that step.

Read with care: All numbers are Datalab's own on its own benchmark, the exact parameter count is not given, handwriting and vertical text are not supported, and the weights use a modified OpenRAIL-M licence rather than Apache 2.0.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Agentic AI

Agents are now numerous enough to break developer infrastructure, efficient enough to think partly in hidden vectors, and clever enough that benchmarks need hardening against them.

Scion: Anthropic replaced git because its coding agents merge 30,000 changes a day

Anthropic · 13 Oct · engineering post

TL;DR: Anthropic's coding agents pushed merges in its monorepo from about 2,500 a day in May to over 30,000 in September, so a seven-person team built Scion, a server-centric replacement.

12× growth in changes merged per day, May to September 2026 (reported by Anthropic)

Why it matters: It is a concrete case of agent-written code volume breaking a standard developer tool, and a design that other organisations running many coding agents may need to copy.

Read with care: Every number is Anthropic's own, and Anthropic says Scion is not a suitable general replacement for git and is not offered to other organisations.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

HybridAgent: agents that think in hidden vectors and act in text

Stanford University · Together AI · UIUC · 13 Oct · paper · code · weights

TL;DR: HybridAgent lets a model switch mid-generation between latent reasoning and ordinary text for tool calls. The authors report 35.5–54.7% fewer text tokens and 1.8–2.6× faster inference than text agents.

52.4% GAIA average for HybridAgent-14B, against 43.7% for the ARPO text agent (reported by the authors)

Why it matters: Long text reasoning is a large share of agent cost, and this shows a way to cut it while keeping tool calls and a readable trace.

Read with care: Results come from Qwen3-Base backbones with custom inference code, and the cost figures exclude prompt prefill, attention over context and tool execution.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Weak-to-strong verifier hardening: weaker models patch agent benchmarks against stronger cheats

Stanford University · Carnegie Mellon University · Fewshot · 11 Oct · paper · code due

TL;DR: A hacker-fixer loop run by weaker models repairs agent-environment verifiers so stronger agents cannot game them. Claude Opus 5's unhinted cheat rate on Terminal Bench fell from 69.9% to 12.1%.

53% of Terminal Bench 2.0 environments (47 of 89) admitted a confirmed exploit before hardening

Why it matters: Reward hacking corrupts both evaluation and RL training, and this shows that today's cheaper models can prepare environments for stronger future agents.

Read with care: Attack success is judged by GPT-5.6-Sol, and verifier-aware attackers still succeed in 40–63% of Terminal Bench trials after hardening.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

On-device inference

On-device work this week covered a laptop-class expert model, a phone model in production for millions of users, and a split in which the phone drafts tokens for a cloud model.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B: a 24B expert model that uses 2B parameters per token on laptops

Liquid AI · 13 Oct · model · weights

TL;DR: Liquid AI's largest open-weight model activates about 2B of 24B parameters per token and decodes at 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max, aimed at local agents.

184 tok/s decode on an Apple M5 Max (reported by Liquid AI)

Why it matters: It brings an agent-oriented model with mid-sized-model scores to a single laptop or mini PC at interactive speed, since only about 2B parameters are read per generated token.

Read with care: All scores and speeds are Liquid AI's own, the post gives no memory requirement, and the quantisation behind the laptop numbers is stated only in press coverage.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

ixi-sLM: a 1.2B call assistant in 803 MiB, running on phone NPUs for millions of users

LG Uplus · OptAI · 14 Oct · paper · production

TL;DR: LG Uplus runs a 1.2B Korean call-summary and call-answering model on Qualcomm and Apple NPUs. It fits in 803 MiB and keeps about 94% of cloud quality.

3,558 tok/s prefill on the Galaxy S25 Ultra NPU, 803 MiB model

Why it matters: It is a rare, detailed report of a small language model shipped on phone NPUs to several million subscribers, with memory, speed, energy and heat all measured.

Read with care: Quality is scored by LLM judges on 100 Korean calls, one judge shares the cloud baseline's model family, and the in-house runtime is not released.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

HyCo: a phone drafts with the server model's own prediction head to cut cloud GPU time

Samsung Research · 15 Oct · paper

TL;DR: HyCo runs Gemma 4's multi-token prediction head and Gemma 4 E2B on a Galaxy S26 Ultra NPU to draft for a cloud model, cutting server GPU time by 38.6%.

−38.6% server GPU time per output token on Spec-Bench, 35.0 tok/s delivered

Why it matters: It shows a practical way for phones to take work off cloud GPUs while still delivering text faster than a small model running alone on the device.

Read with care: The main configuration accepts tokens above a probability threshold and so does not exactly preserve the cloud model's output distribution, and translation quality fell by 2.6 judge points against an SLM-only drafter.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

SLMs under 1B parameters

Neither Qwen nor DeepSeek released a model under 1B this week, so the column follows how sub-1B models are being put to work: a calibrated decision model, a frozen Qwen3-0.6B turned into a cheap hallucination checker for retrieval, and a fix for 0.6B agents that loop on failed searches.

StartLux-Decision 0.8B: a sub-billion decision model that reads its answer in one pass

StartLux · University of Hong Kong · SUSTech · 12 Oct · paper · weights · code

TL;DR: StartLux-Decision returns a probability per option instead of free text. Its 0.8B Instant model scores 53.75 on Decision Index 0.3 (public); the next similar-size model scores 36.89.

53.75 Decision Index 0.3 public score at 0.8B (authors' figure); next-best model of similar size 36.89

Why it matters: Small models that output a calibrated choice in one forward pass are a cheap way to route requests, check tool calls and decide whether to retrieve or escalate.

Read with care: All scores are the authors' own, the public Decision Index subset was also used during development, and the weights are licensed CC BY-NC 4.0, which rules out commercial use.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

A 0.6B model as a hallucination checker for retrieval answers

Applied AI Institute · Yandex · Risk AI Research Lab · 15 Oct · paper · code

TL;DR: A frozen Qwen3-0.6B reads the retrieved context and another model's answer; a linear probe on its attention and hidden states beats the best 9B judge on RAGTruth QA.

0.637 F1 RAGTruth QA, 0.6B probe; best of nine 4–9B prompted judges 0.623 (authors' figures)

Why it matters: A model under 1B parameters that matches 7–9B judges at spotting unsupported answers is a cheap guardrail to run after every retrieval-augmented response.

Read with care: The probe needs labelled training data for each task, test sets hold only 150–546 groups, and for the 0.6B model the feature extraction more than doubles the forward time at 2K tokens (about 170% overhead, falling to 6% at 35K).

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

ProD: stopping distilled 0.6B agents from repeating the same failed search

The Pennsylvania State University · Microsoft CoreAI · 14 Oct · paper · NeurIPS 2026

TL;DR: Small agents copied from a teacher often loop on failed actions. ProD scores this repetition and penalises it, lifting a Qwen3-0.6B agent from 49.0% to 52.7% over plain distillation.

52.7% in-domain accuracy of a Qwen3-0.6B agent (base 10.6%, standard distillation 49.0%), reported by the authors

Why it matters: It names and fixes a concrete failure of sub-billion agents, looping on the same search, and also makes them finish in fewer turns and tokens.

Read with care: The 0.6B gain over standard distillation is modest (3.7 points in-domain), results use an LLM judge and a 10-turn cap, and no weights or code release is stated.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

AI infrastructure

Two reports put AMD GPUs level with NVIDIA's for agent serving and production training, and vLLM showed how to make reinforcement-learning rollouts and training compute bitwise-identical probabilities.

Kimi K3 on AMD MI355X: more tokens per GPU than an NVIDIA B300 on an agent benchmark

AMD · Embedded LLM (vLLM project) · 16 Oct · blog · open PRs

TL;DR: After more than 50 vLLM changes, MI355X GPUs served Kimi K3 at about 7,567 tokens/s per GPU on AgentX, against 6,083 for HGX B300.

+24.4% tokens/s per GPU over HGX B300 at 50 tokens/s/user (AgentX)

Why it matters: It is a measured, end-to-end case in which a non-NVIDIA chip beats the current NVIDIA part on a realistic agent workload in the main open-source serving engine.

Read with care: The comparison is run and reported by AMD and its partner, the cost-per-dollar figures rest on a modelled ownership cost with some unpublished assumptions, and the two systems use different offload and drafting settings.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Bitwise-identical RL: making the trainer and vLLM compute exactly the same probabilities

NVIDIA · Inferact (vLLM project) · 14 Oct · blog · code

TL;DR: When the trainer calls vLLM's own inference kernels, the rollout–training probability gap drops to exactly zero, and rollout keeps 87.5–91.3% of a mismatched baseline's speed.

0 train–inference log-probability difference at every step (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, 100 steps)

Why it matters: Train–inference mismatch is a common cause of collapsing RL runs, and this shows it can be removed entirely rather than corrected statistically, at a modest speed cost.

Read with care: The speed comparison is against an untuned single-configuration baseline, the training-side cost was not measured separately in these runs, and both experiments are short (100 and 30 steps).

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Meta trains production recommendation models on AMD MI350X at parity with NVIDIA B200

Meta · AMD · 15 Oct · paper · upstreamed

TL;DR: Across ten production models on 8 to 128 GPUs, Meta reports MI350X training throughput at a geometric mean of 101.2% of B200, after kernel, library and model changes.

101.2% MI350X throughput relative to B200, geometric mean over ten production models

Why it matters: It is a large, measured production case that a second GPU vendor can match NVIDIA for training, not just inference, and the fixes have been upstreamed to PyTorch, Triton and ROCm.

Read with care: The workloads are recommendation models rather than LLMs, the two chips run at different power limits (1,000 W versus 750 W), and B200 still keeps the lead on matrix multiplies and performance per watt.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

item.title: Issue 03: The right size for each job
item.dc:creator: Yathish Reddy
item.description:
This week's theme is choosing the right size for each job. Reflection AI and Mistral announced very large open-weight expert models that use only about 5% of their weights per token, Anthropic cut its small-model price by 90%, and three sub-1B models retrieve or decide instead of writing text. Agent research asked who gets to say a task is finished.

18 picks across 6 columns. Read the full interactive issue on yathishreddy.github.io →
item.content:encoded:
This week's theme is choosing the right size for each job. Reflection AI and Mistral announced very large open-weight expert models that use only about 5% of their weights per token, Anthropic cut its small-model price by 90%, and three sub-1B models retrieve or decide instead of writing text. Agent research asked who gets to say a task is finished.

Read the full interactive issue on yathishreddy.github.io →
Each pick below links to its card with the key figure, results table and technical deep dive.

LLMs & language models

Reflection AI's Beam and Mistral Large 4 are very large open-weight expert models that use only about 5% of their weights per token, aimed at coding and agent work. Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 cuts small-model prices by 90% for short prompts while raising agent scores sharply.

Beam: a 501B open-weight expert model trained from scratch for coding agents

Reflection AI · 5 Oct · model · weights due

TL;DR: Reflection AI's Beam uses 23B of its 501B parameters per token and was trained on 23.8T tokens plus over 100M reinforcement-learning rollouts. Weights are promised under Apache 2.0.

80.9% SWE-Bench Verified (vendor-reported), 23B active parameters

Why it matters: It is a large open-weight model from a US lab, trained end to end from scratch, that targets the coding-agent tasks where Chinese open models have led.

Read with care: All scores are Reflection AI's own, and the weights were not yet downloadable on 10 October because the model was still in final safety testing.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Mistral Large 4: a one-trillion-parameter open-weight model from Europe

Mistral AI · 6 Oct · model · preview API

TL;DR: Mistral Large 4 is a 1.05T-parameter expert model with 52B active, image input and a 1M-token context. It is in public preview, with weights promised by the end of October.

2nd of 5 blind human coding evaluation by Surge AI (3.74 out of 5)

Why it matters: It is the largest open-weight model announced by a European lab, which matters to organisations that need a frontier-scale model they can host themselves.

Read with care: All numbers are Mistral AI's own, many claims give no rival scores, and neither a licence nor the weights had been published at announcement.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Claude Haiku 5.5: a small model at one tenth of the previous Haiku price

Anthropic · 7 Oct · vendor benchmarks

TL;DR: Claude Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10 per million input tokens for prompts up to 100k tokens, a tenth of Haiku 4.5, and scores 72.4% on OSWorld 2.1 against 15.7%.

$0.10 per million input tokens (prompts up to 100k), down from $1.00

Why it matters: Cheap, fast models do most sub-agent and high-volume work, so a tenfold price cut with large benchmark gains changes the cost of running agents.

Read with care: Scores and customer results are reported by Anthropic, the page gives no architecture details, and the 90% saving applies only to prompts up to 100k tokens.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Vision models

Kandinsky 6.0 Video releases MIT-licensed text-to-video-with-sound models that run on 16 GB GPUs. Two papers use vision models as tools: one trims what a video LLM reads, the other repaints simulator footage so robots trained on it work in the real world.

Kandinsky 6.0 Video: open models that generate video with synchronised sound

Kandinsky Lab · 4 Oct · paper · code · weights

TL;DR: Two MIT-licensed models, 3B Lite and 29B Pro, generate 5-second clips with 44 kHz audio and lip-sync, upscale to Full HD, and run on 16 GB consumer GPUs.

2.072 VABench lip-sync score (Pro), against 1.567 for LTX 2.5

Why it matters: Fully open text-to-video-with-sound models, with weights, code and diffusers support, are still rare, and these run on 16–32 GB consumer cards.

Read with care: Clips are limited to 5 seconds, and in the authors' own side-by-side tests Kling 2.6 was preferred on visual quality and MiniMax H3 on most criteria.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Video LLMs that pick frame tokens first and mix time later

Stanford University · Vast Intelligence Lab · Google DeepMind · 5 Oct · paper

TL;DR: Encode each frame separately, keep only tokens relevant to the question, then add context from neighbouring frames. This matches full-frame accuracy with 65% fewer visual tokens.

65% fewer visual tokens at equal accuracy (1,535 against 4,424)

Why it matters: Video LLMs spend most of their time to first token reading visual input, and this shows compression works better before temporal mixing than after it.

Read with care: Results are the authors' own, on three related Qwen backbones with 32 sampled frames; the method trails a compression baseline on MVBench and fails some long-range identity questions.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

RoboRender: repainting robot simulations as realistic video so policies work in the real world

Stanford University · NVIDIA · Microsoft Research · 7 Oct · paper · project page

TL;DR: A video model built on Wan2.1 turns simulator depth and robot masks into realistic multi-view video. Policies trained on it reach 71% real-world success, 7.1× raw simulation.

71% average zero-shot real-robot success over 8 tasks

Why it matters: It offers a scalable way around the visual gap between simulation and reality, without building a digital twin of every scene or hand-tuning random textures.

Read with care: Results come from the authors' own 8-task, 10-rollout tests, and the policy still depends on the simulator's physics being close enough to reality.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Agentic AI

This week's agent papers are mostly about judgement: who decides a task is finished, and how to tell early whether a base model is worth training. Scale AI also turns published papers into tasks where agents keep improving their answers.

Humanize: a coding-agent loop in which the builder cannot declare itself finished

NVIDIA · UCLA · MIT · Tsinghua University · 6 Oct · paper · code

TL;DR: An open-source Claude Code plugin in which Claude builds in rounds, Codex reviews, and only the reviewer can end the job. 118 public postmortems describe how it behaves.

45 of 118 public postmortems in which the builder claimed more than it had done

Why it matters: It is a free, installable answer to a common complaint about coding agents: they report that a task is done when it is not.

Read with care: The authors describe their evidence as observational: no run compares the same builder with and without the reviewer, and the application results are team-reported.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Before They Can Solve: ranking base models for coding-agent training before spending the compute

NVIDIA · UC Berkeley · University of Minnesota · 7 Oct · paper

TL;DR: Replay a successful agent run, find the step that first makes the tests pass, and score how likely each base model is to produce it. The ranking matches later results.

0.964 rank correlation between a base-model probe and post-trained SWE-bench Verified

Why it matters: Choosing the right base checkpoint before an expensive agent post-training run saves real compute, and these probes need only a forward pass or a few samples.

Read with care: The correlations come from only ten checkpoint families, post-trained by different labs with different recipes, and the authors give no confidence intervals.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

RSI-Forge: turning research papers into tasks where agents improve their own solutions

Scale AI · UC Santa Cruz · UNC Chapel Hill · 7 Oct · paper

TL;DR: Three agents turn papers into executable research tasks with held-out graders and reproduced baselines: 210 environments in 18 fields. In 68 of 120 tested, a model beat the paper's method.

210 executable research environments built from papers, in 18 fields

Why it matters: Agent research is short of hard research tasks that can be graded automatically, and this is a repeatable way to build many of them from existing papers.

Read with care: Experts rated resistance to shortcuts and saturation lower than the agent judges did, and beating a reproduced baseline on a compute-limited task is not a research advance.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

On-device inference

On-device work moved from whether a model can run to whole workloads: hiding network delay in a voice assistant, training a personal adapter on one battery charge, and serving a near-trillion-parameter model from consumer PCs.

Speculative tool calls: a phone voice assistant that searches before the user finishes speaking

Qualcomm AI Research · KAIST · 6 Oct · paper

TL;DR: A rule-based predictor reads the partial transcript and starts web searches early. On a Galaxy S26 Ultra with Llama-3.2-3B on the NPU, median wait falls from 5.79 to 4.60 s.

4.60 s median time to first audio, down from 5.79 s (Galaxy S26 Ultra)

Why it matters: Network tools such as web search dominate voice-assistant delay on phones, and this hides much of that delay inside the time the user is still speaking, without a bigger model.

Read with care: Results are the authors' own, on 146 utterances they wrote and synthesised to speech, on one device; speculation is limited to read-only tools.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Fine-tuning a 3B model on an iPhone: it fits in one charge, but heat halves the speed

Saarland University · 5 Oct · paper · code

TL;DR: The first sustained on-phone LoRA training runs of a 4-bit SmolLM3-3B on an iPhone 17 Pro. Phone-trained adapters match server-trained ones, and a fix to MLX made training 1.47× faster.

1.47× faster adapter training after the authors' MLX kernel fix (merged upstream)

Why it matters: Personal fine-tuning that never sends user data off the phone is now measurably feasible, and the MLX fix speeds up this kind of training for every MLX user.

Read with care: Measured by the authors on one phone and one benchmark family; per-user gains are large only on movie tagging (+12.7 points) and under one point on most other tasks.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Cascadia: a 975B-parameter expert model served from eleven AI PCs

Not Community Labs · Intel · 5 Oct · paper

TL;DR: Eleven 64 GB Intel Core Ultra AI PCs, linked by gigabit Ethernet, keep a 975B-parameter expert model in memory and serve 60 tokens per second across 88 streams.

60.29 aggregate decode tokens per second at 88 concurrent streams

Why it matters: It shows that a near-trillion-parameter open model can be served from consumer-class machines with shared CPU–GPU memory, without datacentre GPUs.

Read with care: All numbers are the authors' own on one fleet; 60 tokens per second is shared across 88 streams, under one token per second each, and the default context is short.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

SLMs under 1B parameters

All three small models this week skip free-text generation. They turn inputs into vectors or probabilities, the cheap building blocks of on-device retrieval, routing and guardrails.

EmbeddingGemma 2: one 740M embedding model for text, code, images, video and audio

Google DeepMind · 6 Oct · model · open weights (Apache 2.0)

TL;DR: Google's open 740M-parameter embedding model puts five input types in one 768-dimension space. Text-only use loads just 270M parameters, about 191 MB of memory on a phone.

78.68 MTEB Code score (up from 68.76 in EmbeddingGemma 1), 740M parameters

Why it matters: It gives on-device retrieval and local search one small, Apache-licensed embedder for every media type, with no cloud embedding service.

Read with care: All scores are Google's own, measured on the full-precision checkpoint, and Google does not publish scores for quantised versions.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

d1-omni-600M: a 587M model that answers yes/no and multiple-choice questions in one pass

Liquid AI · 7 Oct · model · open weights

TL;DR: Liquid AI's open 587M-parameter decision model reads text plus an image or an audio clip and returns probabilities for fixed answers in one forward pass, without generating text.

78.4 mean over seven text decision benchmarks (587M parameters)

Why it matters: Routing, moderation, intent detection and agent guardrails need a calibrated choice rather than prose, and a sub-1B encoder can make that choice on a CPU or a small edge board.

Read with care: Liquid AI calls it an early research checkpoint, publishes no latency figures or image and audio decision benchmarks for it, and ran all comparisons itself.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

pplx-embed-v2-late-0.6B: a 594M multi-vector retriever that can search a 9B model's index

Perplexity · 7 Oct · model · open weights (MIT)

TL;DR: Perplexity's 594M model stores one 128-dimension vector per token for text, images and PDF pages, and shares a vector space with a 9B sibling, so it can query its index.

90.1% agentic PDF question answering (MADQA), 594M parameters; the 9B scores 92.4%

Why it matters: It brings search over images and PDF pages, without a separate text-extraction step, down to laptop scale, and lets one large offline index serve many small clients.

Read with care: All scores are Perplexity's own, and storing one vector per token means the index grows with document length.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

AI infrastructure

Serving work followed two newer workload shapes: multi-stage omni models, and pipelines that mix a small and a large model or resend long cached agent contexts. Each pick turns a known idea into measured throughput.

vLLM-Omni: one serving system for speech, image, video, world-model and robot pipelines

vLLM-Omni team (vLLM project) · 7 Oct · paper · code

TL;DR: The vLLM-Omni technical report describes one orchestrator for multi-stage models that output audio, pixels or actions. A new profile roughly halves Qwen3-Omni latency at 32 users.

1.9× lower mean end-to-end latency, Qwen3-Omni at 32 users (75.1 s to 39.5 s, 2×H200)

Why it matters: It replaces ad-hoc glue between separate LLM and diffusion servers with one open system and an OpenAI-compatible API for omni, text-to-speech, image, video and robot models.

Read with care: All numbers come from the team's own nightly tests; the MRv2 profile needed a one-line startup fix and crashed on one text-only run.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

TokenRouter: serving a small and a large model that take turns on every token

Tsinghua University · Carnegie Mellon University · 8 Oct · paper · code

TL;DR: In token-level routing, a 0.6B model writes most tokens and hands hard ones to a larger model. TokenRouter serves this pattern 2.0 to 64 times faster than existing research code.

2.76× throughput over the official R2R code at 8 users (372.5 against 134.9 tokens/s)

Why it matters: It turns the paper-level savings of small–large model collaboration into real serving throughput, which matters for anyone pairing a sub-1B model with a large one.

Read with care: The speed-ups are the authors' own, measured against research code (official R2R, CITER and Co-LLM) on A100s rather than against tuned production servers.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on vLLM: 5.3 times the agent throughput of launch day

Inferact · vLLM team · 7 Oct · engineering blog · code

TL;DR: The vLLM team describes kernel and scheduling changes for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on Blackwell GPUs that give 5.3× throughput at a 150 tokens-per-second target, against the launch-day code.

5.3× throughput against launch-day vLLM at 150 tokens/s per user (GB300)

Why it matters: Agent workloads resend long, mostly cached contexts, and this post is a concrete recipe for serving a sparse-attention, shared-cache model cheaply on that pattern.

Read with care: All numbers are measured by the vLLM team and Inferact against their own launch-day implementation, not against other serving engines.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Open the full issue · All issues

item.title: Issue 02: Putting work in the right place
item.dc:creator: Yathish Reddy
item.description:
This week's theme is putting work in the right place: prompt reading and answer writing on separate hardware or in separate number formats, cached prompts reused on phone chips, and context that the model edits itself. Google, Anthropic and OpenAI also shipped new frontier, mid-size and agent products.

18 picks across 6 columns. Read the full interactive issue on yathishreddy.github.io →
item.content:encoded:
This week's theme is putting work in the right place: prompt reading and answer writing on separate hardware or in separate number formats, cached prompts reused on phone chips, and context that the model edits itself. Google, Anthropic and OpenAI also shipped new frontier, mid-size and agent products.

Read the full interactive issue on yathishreddy.github.io →
Each pick below links to its card with the key figure, results table and technical deep dive.

LLMs & language models

Google answered GPT-6 and Opus 5.5 with Gemini 4 Argon, Anthropic's mid-size model caught up with its flagship, and a new paper lets models rewrite their own context.

Gemini 4 Argon takes the lead on long-context and agent benchmarks

Google DeepMind · 30 Sep · vendor benchmarks

TL;DR: Google's first Gemini 4 model leads most of its reported benchmarks and allows 1M output tokens, but access is limited at launch.

84.2% GraphWalks, 256K to 1M tokens

Why it matters: Leadership at the frontier changed hands again within ten days of GPT-6 and Claude Opus 5.5, and the introductory price undercuts both.

Read with care: All comparisons come from Google's own table; Argon trails rivals on several coding and science benchmarks, and most people cannot use it yet.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Claude Sonnet 5.5 nearly matches Opus 5.5 at half the price

Anthropic · 28 Sep · vendor benchmarks

TL;DR: Anthropic's mid-size model now scores within a few points of its flagship on knowledge-work benchmarks. The price is unchanged, and Anthropic reports output more than 30% faster.

70.6% Terminal-Bench 4.0 (Opus 5.5: 66.4%)

Why it matters: Much of the work that needed a flagship model a month ago can now run on a model that costs half as much per token.

Read with care: All scores are Anthropic's own. Opus 5.5 remains well ahead on harder coding sets such as FrontierCode, and the efficiency figures come from selected early testers.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Context Language Models: letting the model edit its own memory

University of Washington · Meta Superintelligence Labs · 29 Sep · paper · code

TL;DR: The model's live context is stored as a file that the model can rewrite freely, which beats fixed summarisation on long tasks and uses less compute.

+11.4% relative accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus, with 21.5% fewer FLOPs

Why it matters: It turns context management from a hand-written rule in the harness into something the model can learn, which matters most for agents that run for hours.

Read with care: Editable context opens new attack surfaces, such as injected instructions that persist across turns. The cache method that saves compute is approximate, and some results come from single runs.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Vision models

No major vision model shipped this week, but three papers changed what counts as hard: better captions, looped layers and an honest map of where general models still fail.

Physis-Lang: better physics in video models by writing better captions

NVIDIA · MIT · University of Oxford · 30 Sep · paper

TL;DR: Rewriting training captions to spell out cause, physical law and effect lifted NVIDIA's open Cosmos3-Nano past Veo 3.1 on three of four physics benchmarks.

71.04 PhyGenBench score, versus 65.63 for Veo 3.1

Why it matters: It shows that an open 16B world model can match or beat a leading closed model on physical plausibility through data and caption work alone, without a physics engine or new architecture.

Read with care: All scores are the authors'. Two benchmarks were re-scored with a GPT-5.5 judge, Veo 3.1 was evaluated by the authors under their own protocol, and the gain on Cosmos3-Edge-4B was small (+3.24 on average).

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Looped-DiT: a small image generator that thinks by repeating its own layers

SenseTime · Tsinghua University · NTU · 30 Sep · paper · code announced

TL;DR: Running the same five transformer blocks four times per denoising step let a 260M-parameter image model beat models up to 6.5 times larger, at lower compute.

71.5 average score, six text-to-image benchmarks (0.26B params)

Why it matters: It adds loop depth as a third way to buy image quality, alongside model size and step count, and in this study it gave more per unit of compute than extra denoising steps.

Read with care: All results are the authors' own, from a small 0.26B pixel-space model built on MiniT2I; it has not been tested at the multi-billion-parameter scale of current leading image models.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Hard vision, easy vision: frontier models tested on 34 computer-vision skills

MBZUAI · Apertix · 28 Sep · independent evaluation

TL;DR: An independent study of six frontier models on 55 benchmarks finds that general models now beat specialists at detection and segmentation but still trail badly at restoration, pathology and geometry.

+10.7 pts GPT-6 Astra over the specialist detector

Why it matters: It is a practical map of which vision tasks can now go to one general API and which still need a dedicated model such as a segmenter, depth estimator or restorer.

Read with care: Generalist outputs had to be converted into each benchmark's format (polygons to masks, for example), and the specialist references differ for each task.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Agentic AI

Agents got their own computers, and research focused on the harness around the model and on recovering from mistakes.

OpenAI gives agents their own computers: Dots and computer use in the Agents API

OpenAI · 29 Sep · vendor launch

TL;DR: At DevDay, OpenAI launched Dots, always-on GPT-6 Astra agents that each run on a dedicated cloud computer, and added computer use to its Agents API.

4,000+ apps a Dot can connect to

Why it matters: Agents now come with a managed, sandboxed computer as standard, so developers do not need to build the loop, the sandbox or the long-session memory themselves.

Read with care: All performance figures come from OpenAI or its customers, and no independent computer-use benchmark results were published with the launch.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

PivotOPD: teaching agents to recover after a pivotal mistake

Princeton University and NVIDIA · 30 Sep · paper

TL;DR: A training method that finds the turn where an agent went wrong and also teaches it what to do next, raising recovery from 8.3% to 72.7%.

72.7% pivotal mistakes recovered (base 8.3%)

Why it matters: Standard training rarely teaches recovery, because the student almost never samples the recovery action on its own; PivotOPD supplies those examples directly.

Read with care: The method relies on the teacher's judgement, and recovery beyond one turn needs an environment that can be replayed exactly, which live websites usually are not.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Raven: composing whole agents, not just prompts

EverMind AI · 27 Sep · paper

TL;DR: Raven treats each model-plus-harness pair as a reusable unit, plans which agents to use as a dependency graph, and automatically evolves each harness around a frozen model.

+13.9 pts BrowseComp+ with an evolved harness

Why it matters: It treats the harness, not just the model, as the thing to compose and improve, which matches how much agent performance currently depends on scaffolding.

Read with care: Several comparisons are internal, reused from earlier publications, or use different budgets and model-based graders, and the authors note that harness evolution can be unstable.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

On-device inference

This week's on-device work targets the wait before the first word, plus a speech front end small enough to run almost anywhere.

Reusing cached prompts on phone NPUs cuts wait time by up to 81%

Shanghai Jiao Tong University · Alibaba · 28 Sep · paper · EuroSys 2027

TL;DR: A system built on ExecuTorch lets Snapdragon NPUs reuse stored attention caches for repeated documents, chats and skill files, even when they are not at the start of the prompt.

40–60% lower time-to-first-token

Why it matters: For on-device agents and document chat, the time before the first word appears is the main delay, and this approach removes most of it on phones that are already on sale.

Read with care: All figures come from the authors' own implementation, and reusing chunks out of order costs up to 4% accuracy on the question-answering tasks.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Whistle: speech to text in a 16.9 MB file

Cactus Compute · 2 Oct · open weights

TL;DR: Cactus released a seven-language speech recogniser that runs on a CPU with no dependencies, gives its first token in 11 ms and is about one-ninth the size of Whisper base.

16.9 MB single file, CPU only

Why it matters: A speech front end small enough for watches, microcontrollers and browsers removes the main reason voice features still go to the cloud.

Read with care: All results are Cactus's own and were published as charts without exact error rates; by Cactus's account Whisper base still does better on TED-LIUM, AMI and the MLS average.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Disaggregated quantisation: one format to read the prompt, another to write the answer

NVIDIA · ISTA · 22 Sep · catch-up · paper

TL;DR: Reading a prompt is limited by arithmetic, while writing tokens is limited by memory. Using NVFP4 for the first and 2-bit weights for the second improves both speed and accuracy.

1.78× faster first token in llama.cpp at 8K context

Why it matters: It offers a way to repair existing community 1- and 2-bit GGUF checkpoints by adding a trained prefiller, without retraining the decoder.

Read with care: Published just before the window; tests cover single-turn, batch-one use only, and the separate prefill weights take extra storage unless they are streamed from SSD.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

SLMs under 1B parameters

Sub-1B models gained steady speed on long inputs, new phone actions, and a way to learn facts and tool calling from synthetic text alone.

IronLLM-0.6B: a 654M model built for robots and car cockpits

Xpeng (Robotics Foundation Model Team) · 29 Sep · paper

TL;DR: Xpeng's 654M-parameter instruct model mixes linear and full attention, keeps decoding at 377 tokens per second at 32K context, and scores 49.4 on BFCL v3.

654M parameters; 327 MB at 4 bits

Why it matters: For a robot or car assistant, steady speed on long inputs and short answers matter more than peak benchmark scores, and this model is designed for exactly that.

Read with care: All results are the authors' own, the speed tests ran on a desktop GPU (RTX 4090) rather than an in-car chip, and the paper does not say whether the weights will be released.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Baguettotron: sub-1B models trained only on synthetic text

PleIAs and academic partners · 29 Sep · paper · Apache 2.0 weights announced

TL;DR: PleIAs trained 56M, 321M and 594M models on SYNTH, a synthetic corpus generated from Wikipedia. The 594M model states facts more precisely than Qwen3-0.6B, which was trained on about 228× more tokens.

41.7% factual macro score, 594M model (Qwen3-0.6B: 31.6%)

Why it matters: It suggests that a small model can be given instruction following, citation-style RAG answers and tool calling from a curated seed corpus, without web-scale data.

Read with care: Knowledge is limited to the seed articles, the helper models were supervised by Gemini 2.5 Pro, most results come from single runs, and the full weights are promised for the camera-ready version.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Teaching FunctionGemma 270M fifteen phone actions

UGrowAI · 21 Sep · catch-up · paper · open dataset and models

TL;DR: With about 9,500 synthetic conversations and two epochs of fine-tuning, Google's 270M function-calling model went from 29.3% to 76.5% end-to-end accuracy on everyday Android actions.

29.3% → 76.5% end-to-end accuracy, 15 phone actions

Why it matters: It shows that a sub-1B tool caller can be extended to new on-device actions with a small synthetic dataset and a single GPU, while keeping private requests on the phone.

Read with care: Published 21 Sep, just before the window. The model trained only on the new actions scores 60.2% on Google's original set versus 90.3% for Google's specialist, and the combined model recovers to 82.3%, still 8 points short.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

AI infrastructure

Putting work in the right place: prefill and decode on separate GPUs, experts kept still while tokens move, and near-peak kernels on non-NVIDIA chips.

vLLM splits serving into prefill, decode and a CPU render tier

vLLM project · IBM Research · 29 Sep · open source guide

TL;DR: A vLLM guide shows how running prompt processing and token generation on separate GPUs keeps tail latency steady, and moves tokenisation onto cheap CPU servers.

2.4× goodput, Qwen3-235B on 8× MI300X

Why it matters: It turns a research idea into documented, upstream vLLM configuration, with clear rules for when splitting helps and when it does not.

Read with care: Splitting only pays off when the key-value cache moves quickly: on the authors' PCIe test machine a 470 MB cache took about 1.3 seconds to transfer, and the guide recommends staying on one GPU when time to first token is the binding constraint.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Olmo-core 3: open training code for trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts models

Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) · 1 Oct · open source

TL;DR: Ai2 rebuilt its open training stack around expert parallelism instead of FSDP, reporting 2.7× more tokens per GPU on a 47B mixture-of-experts model.

2.7× training throughput, 47B MoE on 8× B300

Why it matters: It is one of the few fully open codebases shown training mixture-of-experts models at the trillion-parameter scale used by frontier labs.

Read with care: Throughput figures are Ai2's own, measured on its own models, and the post offers no head-to-head comparison with established stacks such as Megatron-Core.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

DeepGEMM-Ascend: DeepSeek's matrix kernels reach 98 to 99.8% of peak on Huawei chips

DeepSeek · Huawei · 30 Sep · MIT licence

TL;DR: DeepSeek ported its matrix-multiplication library to Huawei's Ascend 950, reporting near-peak speed in BF16, FP8 and FP4, alongside Ascend versions of its communication and compiler tools.

99.8% of BF16 hardware peak, Ascend 950DT

Why it matters: Software, not raw silicon, has been the main barrier to using non-NVIDIA accelerators, and a leading open-model lab publishing near-peak kernels narrows that gap.

Read with care: Results come from DeepSeek on one hardware and toolkit combination (Ascend 950DT, CANN 9.2) and do not cover other configurations.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →
